Can I ask you something? You told me once that your English used to be better. What happened?
It was a chain, really. At sixteen I moved to Franca to play basketball, and the move led to a completely new routine, with training twice a day.
And English didn't fit in that routine.
Exactly. I stopped my classes because of the schedule, and that had a knock-on effect I didn't see coming. With no classes, I stopped watching series in English, too.
That happened to me with Spanish. I studied it for six years back in Chicago, then I got my first job and stopped. Now I can read a menu, and that's about it.
So you know the vicious circle. I speak less because I feel rusty, and I feel rusty because I speak less. Honestly, most of my frustration stems from that.
But you're breaking it now. Twice a week, every week. What made you come back?
The cursinho, actually. I had to read texts in English for the exams, and that brought about a small surprise: I still understood a lot. That, in turn, made me want the rest back.

When a city has a traffic problem, the first idea is almost always the same: build more lanes. It sounds logical. More space should lead to less traffic. But in city after city, the opposite happens. A new lane makes driving faster for a few months. As a result, more people decide to drive, and some people who used to take the bus go back to their cars. Within a few years, the traffic returns, and sometimes it is worse. Planners call this induced demand, and it stems from a simple fact: people react to the change you make. The plan backfires not because the engineers were bad, but because they treated the problem as a question of space. The root cause was never the size of the road. It was the number of people who had no other good way to get to work.

When students explain causes, I see the same three problems. The first is direction. Result in and result from look almost the same, but they point in opposite directions. The move resulted in a new routine. The new routine resulted from the move. Draw the arrow in your head before you speak. The second problem is the word after the connector. Because is followed by a full clause: because I moved. Because of and due to are followed by a noun: because of the move. The third problem is the most interesting one. Students give me one cause for everything. Real life is rarely that simple. Say it was one factor, or the main factor, and your listener will trust you more. A good explanation is not a straight line. It is a chain, and every link has to hold.
